title: Al-'Adl, the Just
hookLine: the Just, who never wrongs anyone
tomorrow: thrown in a well, sold, jailed. where was the kindness?

lines: FAIR IS EASY WHEN IT'S FREE.
YOUR OWN SIDE ASKS FOR EXTRA.
A GIFT THE PROPHET WOULDN'T SIGN.
cards: Splitting a pizza between siblings. Picking teams at recess. Choosing whose group-chat message gets the quick reply.
Fairness is easy when it costs nothing. The hard version shows up when your own side is the one asking for extra. Yesterday's question: fair, even against your own family?
There's a verse that says yes, word for word, and a moment when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, turned down a father who asked him to sign off on a gift.

teach.b: The verse first, from Surah an-Nisa, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred."
Yourselves comes first in the list. Then the father.
A man named Bashir gave one of his sons, an-Nu'man, a gift, and brought him to the Prophet to witness it. Did you give each of your children the same? the Prophet asked. No.

Then fear Allah, he said, and be just between your children. And the gift was taken back. That's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the Prophet declined to witness a present because a brother had been left out.
Behind both stands today's Name. Al-'Adl, the Just, who never wrongs anyone.
In a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet reports from Allah, Allah says He has forbidden injustice for Himself and made it forbidden among people, so do not wrong one another.
The Qur'an says Allah does not wrong anyone by even a speck's weight. So fairness here isn't only a good policy. It's a reflection of who God is, practiced at the dinner table first.

how: Muslims hold that Allah is never unjust and that fairness is owed to everyone, even against oneself and one's family; parents are taught to treat their children evenly in gifts.

o: the Just, who never wrongs anyone
the one who favors His own people
the one who repays harm with harm

games.q: who said what about fairness — tap the pairs.
p: staunch in justice, even against yourselves

s: justice in Islam means loyalty to your own side first
the verse names yourselves, parents and kindred: be just even against them.
the Prophet declined to witness a gift given to only one child
be just between your children, he said, and the gift was taken back.

games.q: you're babysitting two little cousins. one big cookie, one small. the one you like more asks first. what does the Nu'man story point to?
o: the big one to whoever asked first; that's the rule.
the big one to the one who behaved better today.
even it out: split both, or one cuts and the other picks.
games.why: be just between your children, the Prophet told a father. fairness among the small ones is where it starts, and it's a sentence a parent can say at dinner.

practice: Pick one small place in your week where things run a little uneven: who always does the dishes, who always gets the front seat, whose message you always answer last.
Name the fair version, name what keeps getting in the way, and choose one small step that evens it out. Then let it rest for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Adl. The Just, who never wrongs anyone, and who forbade injustice for Himself.

orig.note: Arabic: the Just. listed among the Names in Jami' at-Tirmidhi.

carryVoice: Your line: never unjust, not toward strangers and not in favor of your own. Day fifteen-oh-three, done.

sources.q: O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2587; Sahih Muslim 1623 (an-Nu'man ibn Bashir's gift: be just between your children)
Sahih Muslim 2577 (hadith qudsi: I have forbidden injustice for Myself)
